newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bunds pare gains, dealers say no sell-off in sight.
newsitem.headline: Bunds pare gains, dealers say no sell-off in sight.

text.p: German Bunds gave up some gains in late trading after failing to move convincingly above the key 97.00 level but traders remained unruffled saying no immediate sell-off was in sight.
Bunds were trading up four basis points at 96.84, just above the day's low of 96.82 and off the 97.05 high late in the Frankfurt trading at 1431 GMT.

"I think we will drift sideways in a narrow range between 96.75 and 97.00 until U.S. inflation nubmers are released on Thursday," one dealer forecast for Wednesday. Analysts put support at 96.77 and resistance at 97.00 and 97.06.
"It is really quiet in the cash market with everything being defined by the futures market," another dealer added, saying that the calm should hold at least through the next session.
Meanwhile dealers explained that the long end of the market failed to breach the key 97.00 level convincingly as the market lacked sufficient momentum to move higher.
"Buyers are more interested in middle maturities and the is what is keeping the curve steep but the long end below the key 97.00 level," a dealer said.
Meanwhile dealers also said the dollar's strength has not made much of an impact on the market.
"Basically the short end is ignoring the news, and right now it seems that all news is good news, the market is actually a little bit blind," another dealer added.
The sense the news is good now, however, may quickly evaporate, leaving the market vulnerable to move lower quite quickly, dealers added.

By the afternoon the market had largely shrugged off comments made late on Monday by Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke that slower M3 money supply growth could prompt the Bundesbank to consider nudging interest rates lower again.
The comments this morning helped move the market higher but dealers said the impact had waned by the afternoon.
Meanwhile the market was looking ahead to Thursday's U.S. economic data, noting that it was difficult to predict how the German market would react.
"We have outperformed the U.S. market for some time, and now we have to see how the market will react if the data is good, I don't think that we could move that much higher," a dealer said.
